শিশুখাদ্য, যৌনতা ও নিজের শরীর নিয়ে নারীর: Infant feeding, sexuality, and women’s freedom to decide about their own bodies
মূল লেখক: বাধন অধিকারী · ভাষা ও বিন্যাস: Original author: Badhon Adhikari · Language and layout editing: Md. Ikramul Haq Khan
একই শরীরকে পরিবার, সমাজ ও বাজার ভিন্নভাব: Family, society, and the market may see the same body differently. But how much space does a woman’s own voice have in decisions about that body?
শিশুর খাদ্য, মায়ের দায়িত্ব: An infant’s food, a mother’s responsibility
বাজার যখন স্তনের অর্থ ঠিক করে: When the market defines the meaning of breasts
এতগুলো অর্থ নারীর শরীরে ঢোকে কীভাবে: How do so many meanings enter a woman’s body?
তাহলে নিজের শরীর নিয়ে নারীর সিদ্ধান্তের: How much freedom, then, does a woman have to decide about her own body?
মানুষ পৃথিবীতে এসে নিজের শরীরের ভাষা শেখ: Before learning the language of their own bodies, people learn to recognize another body after entering the world. That first body is often their mother’s. Through hunger and the taste and smell of breast milk, an infant begins to know the world. This relationship between human infants and breast milk is so old that it seems almost timeless, like nature itself. The psychoanalyst Sigmund Freud also sought a primal bodily experience of satisfaction, touch, and pleasure in breastfeeding. The question is this: while investigating what breasts mean to an infant or a man, did Freud ever investigate what a woman’s two breasts mean to her? And how is that meaning constructed?
মাতৃত্ব নারীর দুই স্তনকে দায়িত্বে পরিণত: Motherhood turns a woman’s breasts into a responsibility. In love and sexuality, they carry intimacy. Male desire may turn them into objects of longing. Society seeks to cover them through discipline, while advertising and consumer markets seek to display them to sell products. The social meaning of the same breasts thus changes repeatedly: infant food or motherhood, sexuality, shame, beauty, labor, or commodities. Women are not the only participants in making these meanings. Family, medicine, the state, patriarchy, and markets are active too. Although a woman physically owns her breasts, authority over their meaning is not hers alone. This is where agency—the freedom to make decisions and put them into practice—becomes an issue.
স্তনের বহুবিধ অর্থের মধ্যে সবচেয়ে পুরোনো: The oldest of the many meanings of breasts is perhaps infant food. WHO and UNICEF recommend starting breastfeeding within an hour of birth and giving only breast milk for the first six months. After six months, they advise continued breastfeeding for two years or longer alongside safe, nutritious complementary foods. These health recommendations, however, can also become symbols of moral instruction. In her 1999 book At the Breast: Ideologies of Breastfeeding and Motherhood in the Contemporary United States, American sociologist Linda M. Blum asks how society constructs an ideal of the “good mother” around the seemingly personal decision of how to feed an infant.
‘ব্রেস্ট ইজ বেস্ট’ (বুকের দুধই সেরা) কথা: When “breast is best” is used in health promotion, its social meaning can extend beyond a recommendation about infant health. Breastfeeding can become a measure of a woman’s love, responsibility, or even how “good” a mother she is. Yet women do not have equal opportunities to follow that ideal. Studying white middle-class mothers alongside Black and white working-class mothers, Blum shows how class, race, and work can give breastfeeding different meanings for different women. Treating one model of motherhood as equally “natural” for everyone obscures mothers without the opportunity to meet it. An unfair belief may then arise that a woman unable to breastfeed is a “bad mother.”
বাংলাদেশে অধিকাংশ শিশুই কোনো না কোনো সময়: Most infants in Bangladesh receive breast milk at some point. Ever receiving it, however, is different from receiving only breast milk during the first six months. According to MICS 2025, 97.8% of the most recent children born during the preceding two years had been breastfed at some point; among infants under six months, exclusive breastfeeding was 56.6%. A mother may breastfeed morning and night, but if her infant receives formula or other food or drink during her eight hours at work, that infant no longer counts as exclusively breastfed. A 2022 study in Frontiers in Public Health analyzing the 2011, 2014, and 2017–18 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Surveys found exclusive breastfeeding rates of 59.1% among employed mothers and 64.6% among mothers not in employment. After adjustment, employed mothers had approximately 24% lower odds of exclusive breastfeeding. Odds are related to probability but are not identical; “24% lower probability” would be inaccurate. The study demonstrates an association, not proof that employment alone caused the difference. Lack of childcare, breastfeeding spaces, storage, or adequate breaks can separate a mother’s wishes from her ability to act on them.
বাধা শুধু কর্মক্ষেত্রে নয়, সন্তান জন্মের: Barriers arise not only at work but also after childbirth. A 2026 WHO–UNICEF statement citing MICS 2025 reported that 30.4% of infants in Bangladesh were breastfed within the first hour. Delivery method, hospital arrangements, health-worker support, family, and later the workplace all relate to opportunities to breastfeed. Alongside a mother’s wishes, we therefore need to consider the support she receives.
পুরুষের যৌন আকাঙ্ক্ষার সঙ্গে নারীর স্তনে: The association of women’s breasts with male sexual desire has become so normalized that we may be encouraged to regard breasts as inherently sexual organs. Yet how inherent is this “inherent” meaning? Which body parts are sexual or attractive, and which breast shapes are considered beautiful or desirable, also have social histories. The sexual significance attributed to an organ varies across societies and time. Clothing, modesty rules, art, and popular culture help construct those meanings. Breasts have physical sensitivity; ideas of attraction, shame, and beauty surrounding them are also shaped by history and culture.
শরীর ও যৌনতা নিয়ে আধুনিক চিন্তায় ফ্রয়েডে: Freud strongly influenced modern thinking about bodies and sexuality. His interpretation is a historical theoretical perspective, rather than an unquestionable truth of current science. He saw breastfeeding as not only satisfying hunger but also providing a primal experience of bodily pleasure and satisfaction. He later emphasized this childhood experience in explaining sexual development. Feminist psychoanalysis subsequently posed a counterquestion: whose theoretical gaze is being used to see women’s desire? Being an object of male desire is different from a woman’s experience of her own sexual body. A woman may experience her breasts sexually, enjoy touch, and wish to be desired by a lover. But is the language through which she experiences her breasts her own creation, or does she learn to recognize her desire through meanings long shaped by male desire?
কোন শরীরকে সুন্দর বা কাম্য বলে মনে করা হ: Culture and power influence which bodies seem beautiful or desirable, how acceptable women’s expression of desire is, and the language through which a woman feels pride, pleasure, or discomfort about her breasts. American feminist philosopher and cultural theorist Susan Bordo explores one aspect of this complexity in Unbearable Weight. In her account, the body is not a passive blank page on which culture writes at will. Women experience their bodies and make their meanings. Yet ideas of beauty, desirability, pride, and discomfort already develop within society. Bodily awareness emerges in the tension between personal experience and social ideals.
নারীর স্তন ঢেকে রাখতে হবে; এমন সামাজিক অ: Bangladesh also exhibits social pressure to keep women’s breasts covered. A woman owns her body and clothing, yet repeatedly hears questions about why she has no scarf, why there is no extra cloth over her clothes, why the scarf has slipped, why she has not covered herself, or why her breasts are visible. Opposite pressures also exist: judging a woman in a burqa as “backward” simply from her dress. A scarf or burqa can thus become more than fabric; it can mark control over women’s bodies. Male-dominated society constructs breasts as centers of sexual attraction and then demands that they be concealed because of that sexual meaning. Yet a woman has the right both to wear a scarf or burqa and not to wear one. She may wear a scarf, hijab, or burqa through religious belief, comfort, or cultural identity—or wish to wear none. How much room does she retain for that wish, and for how long?
পুরুষশাসিত সমাজ যেমন স্তনকে যৌনবস্তু হিস: As male-dominated society sexualizes breasts and controls women’s bodies in the name of keeping them out of sight, the market can exert control from the opposite direction. Advertising and popular culture display women’s bodies to make products attractive. In the same society, however, a woman entering public space in clothing of her choice may face harassment about whether her chest is sufficiently covered. Market visibility and social discipline appear opposed: one conceals breasts, the other displays them for commerce. The underlying question is the same: how much authority does a woman have over her body’s visibility? When expectations of modesty or the market override her decisions, both processes can restrict her agency.
যে স্তনকে শালীনতার নামে আড়াল করতে বলা হচ: The breasts that modesty rules demand be concealed are also an infant’s first food source. Does feeding a hungry child free a woman’s body from social surveillance? A 2022 systematic review in Maternal & Child Nutrition analyzed experiences of more than 17,000 mothers across 71 studies. It found that other people’s gaze, fear of negative reactions, expectations to cover breasts, and cultures viewing breasts primarily as sexual could influence decisions to breastfeed in public.
পুরুষের কামনা যেখানে ব্যক্তিগত আকাঙ্ক্ষা: Where male desire operates as personal longing, markets can translate that longing into commercial language on a larger scale. The history of selling products through women’s sexual appeal is long: breasts become tools for attracting attention to commodities without themselves being the commodity. Food markets create a more complex relationship. Markets do not only sell products using images of breasts; they have also developed around the food breasts produce. Formula, breast pumps, milk-storage bags, bottles, and other products are now part of everyday motherhood and infant feeding.
এখানেই ‘ভালো মা’র প্রশ্নটি ফিরে আসে। একদ: The question of the “good mother” returns here. Medicine and society tell women that exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months is best for infants. Yet not all women receive the time, maternity leave, workplace opportunities to feed, or safe storage needed to act on that choice. Markets offer commercial alternatives to breast milk in precisely this gap.
ফর্মুলাকে কেবল বাজারের তৈরি কৃত্রিম প্রয়: Formula is not simply an artificial need invented by markets. An infant may have medical needs, and a mother’s physical circumstances may make breastfeeding difficult. The question concerns the market’s role in shaping the environment of choice, not formula’s existence. In 2022, WHO described the global formula industry as a US$55 billion market. That year, WHO and UNICEF analyzed experiences of more than 8,500 women and over 300 health professionals in eight countries, including Bangladesh, showing how infant-food marketing uses parental anxiety, scientific and health language, and digital media. Markets therefore help shape not only available products but also why they seem necessary or desirable. A market’s existence does not make a choice false; the existence of choice does not erase market power. For a mother working long hours without opportunities to feed or store milk, where do choice and necessity merge in selecting formula?
মাতৃদুগ্ধের বিকল্পই শুধু পণ্য নয়; মাতৃদু: Breast-milk substitutes are not the only commodities: breast milk itself may enter commercial supply chains. Susan Newman and Michal Nahman’s study “Nurture commodified?” uses experiences from India to examine the roles of women’s care labor, class, and markets. The question is whether collecting and selling milk safeguards women’s consent, recognizes their labor, and distributes benefits fairly.
লুই হেন্ডারসন ও জেন হামফ্রিজ অক্সফোর্ড র: In research published in the Oxford Review of Economic Policy, Louis Henderson and Jane Humphries place breastfeeding within the history of caring labor. Much of this labor remains invisible in conventional economic accounting even though it sustains economic life. Yet the same milk acquires a price when it enters commercial supply chains. The question is then not only who owns the milk, but who has the power to determine its value.
এতক্ষণের আলোচনায় দুই স্তনের অন্তত তিনটি: We have identified at least three social meanings of breasts: food for infants; desire and pleasure in sexuality; and, for markets, either attention-getting devices or opportunities for profit around food and labor. Drawing on Michel Foucault, power does more than prohibit: it also produces knowledge and standards of normality. Social standards of the “good mother,” “desirable woman,” “beautiful body,” or “modest woman” may therefore become part of a woman’s own way of seeing her body.
স্যান্ড্রা লি বার্টকি ফেমিনিনিটি অ্যান্ড: In Femininity and Domination, Sandra Lee Bartky brings Foucault’s ideas to women’s bodies, showing that modern feminine discipline does not always require an external guard. Women learn to monitor their own bodies: am I beautiful, attractive, or modest enough? In motherhood, the question may become: am I a “good enough mother”? Yet the ability to breastfeed may depend on hospitals, family, employment, leave, and workplace infrastructure. Structural barriers can consequently be experienced as personal failure.
একইভাবে যৌনতার ক্ষেত্রেও নারী পরস্পরবিরো: Women face contradictory instructions in sexuality too: be attractive, but do not appear too sexual. Breasts may be displayed in advertisements, while the same breasts must be covered when feeding an infant in public. Motherhood calls for one use of the body, male desire another, and markets yet another. The meanings through which a woman understands her body are thus formed within relationships of power among families, institutions, society, and markets.
নিজের সিদ্ধান্ত নেওয়ার স্বাধীনতাকে শুধু: Reducing agency to the ability to say “no” leaves out much of women’s lives. Wanting to breastfeed is an exercise of agency, as is not wanting to. Choosing to wear a scarf or burqa—and choosing not to—is also agency. A woman has a right to determine how visible or concealed her body will be. Experiencing her breasts sexually, consenting to be part of a lover’s desire or refusing it, and deciding whether to feed, store, or sell her milk also involve agency. But every “I want” should be accompanied by another question: who has shaped the conditions of my wanting?
একজন নারী সন্তানকে একচেটিয়া মাতৃদুগ্ধ দি: One woman wants to breastfeed exclusively but her job prevents it. Another chooses formula because it works best for her. One is comfortable making her breasts sexually visible; another is not. Where does women’s agency go if outsiders judge all these choices against a single moral standard?
সিদ্ধান্তের স্বাধীনতা মানে সব সামাজিক প্: Freedom to decide does not mean being free of every social influence. It means understanding preferences, making decisions, and having opportunities to enact them amid competing pressures. It includes the right to say “yes” as well as “no,” to reject meanings imposed by others, to embrace preferred meanings, and to change a decision.
শিশুর খাদ্য, মাতৃত্বের শ্রম, পুরুষের কাম: Infant food, maternal labor, male desire, women’s own longing, and commodities: none of the many meanings attributed to the same breasts is created by women alone. Yet a woman is not merely a body bearing meanings others have made. Perhaps this is precisely where her agency lies: which meanings others assign to her body she accepts, rejects, changes, or replaces with her own. Those answers define the scope of her freedom to decide.
নিজের পছন্দ আর সামাজিক চাপের মধ্যে পার্থ: Which questions help distinguish personal preference from social pressure?
স্তন্যদানে সহায়তার দায়িত্ব পরিবার, কর্মক: How can families, workplaces, and hospitals share responsibility for supporting breastfeeding?
